title: Lab Design and Safety Numbers: Eyewash, SDS Cut-offs and Room Targets
summary: Fill in a new lab’s floor plan, race a splashed worker to the eyewash in 10 seconds, find which SDS ingredients count, and sort each number into law, guidance or design target.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 1 Hits 11–14 and completes the Number Vault table (design, HVAC, eyewash, exits, sharps and workforce rows here; retention and specimen rows in ops-record-specimen-retention). Corrects the eyewash item (adds the 10-second criterion and the regulation wording) and the SDS threshold wording (≥ cut-offs). Design, sharps and licensure figures are taught as pending reviewer figures.

objectives: Distinguish OSHA requirements (English SDS; eyewash within the work area) from guidance (10-second reach) and design targets.
Apply the SDS mixture cut-offs: usually 1%, 0.1% for carcinogens.
State the reviewer’s room targets (68–76 °F, 20–60% humidity, ≈ 12 air changes per hour) and treat them as design targets.
Distinguish state licensure from national certification.

scenes.title: Designing a safe lab, number by number
scenes.altText: An empty floor plan of a new laboratory appears. Question marks pop up over it: How warm? How much fresh air? Where is the eyewash? How many doors? What must the chemical paperwork say? The cartoon scientist holds a clipboard.

cues.text: A hospital is building a new laboratory. The floor plan is empty.
The architect has questions. How warm should it be? How much fresh air? Where does the eyewash go? How many doors?
And every chemical needs paperwork. The exam asks about these numbers — and about which ones are law and which are design targets.

scenes.title: The room: comfort, air and space
scenes.altText: The floor plan fills in. A thermometer token reads 68–76 °F (about 20–24 °C) and a humidity token 20–60%. Curved air arrows cycle through the room with a counter “about 12 air changes per hour”. Space tokens read 150–200 net sq ft per staff member and 27–40 net sq ft per hospital bed. A grey tag marks all of these as the reviewer’s design targets.

cues.text: Start with the room itself. The reviewer’s design targets keep the lab between 68 and 76 degrees Fahrenheit — about 20 to 24 Celsius.
Relative humidity between 20 and 60 percent. Instruments, reagents and people all work best in a steady room.
Fresh air keeps fumes from building up. The reviewer’s target is about 12 air changes per hour — the room’s air replaced roughly every five minutes.
Space is planned too: about 150 to 200 net square feet per full-time staff member, or 27 to 40 per hospital bed.
These are design targets from the reviewer’s source, not federal law. Real projects follow local building codes and design standards.

props.text: Reviewer’s design targets — check local codes

scenes.title: A splash: the 10-second rule
scenes.altText: A worker at a bench gets a chemical splash. A dotted path leads to an eyewash station while a timer counts up to 10 seconds. A card quotes the OSHA rule: suitable facilities “within the work area for immediate emergency use”. A second card shows the 1992 OSHA letter: no more than 100 feet and reachable within 10 seconds. A note says OSHA treats the ANSI Z358.1 standard as guidance, not as an enforced rule. Then a door icon appears on a second wall: the reviewer’s “two exits for rooms over 100 sq ft”.

cues.text: Now something goes wrong: a corrosive chemical splashes into a worker’s eyes. Every second counts.
The OSHA rule says suitable eyewash facilities must be within the work area, for immediate emergency use. It sets no distance.
A 1992 OSHA letter put numbers on it: no more than 100 feet away, and reachable within 10 seconds. The time matters more than the distance — a blinded person must get there fast.
OSHA treats the ANSI eyewash standard as helpful guidance, not as an enforced rule. Exams usually quote the 10-second idea.
The reviewer adds that rooms over 100 square feet need two exits, so a fire cannot block the only way out. Exit rules really depend on the fire code in force.

props.text: ANSI Z358.1 = guidance OSHA may refer to, not an enforced rule
Exits: reviewer’s rule — fire codes decide

scenes.title: In the lab: the SDS, sharps and the workforce
scenes.altText: A Safety Data Sheet with 16 numbered sections flips open; Section 3 (ingredients) is highlighted. A mixture beaker shows two ingredients: one at 0.5% marked carcinogen (counts, because the cut-off for carcinogens is 0.1%) and one at 0.5% irritant (below the usual 1% cut-off). An “English” stamp lands on the sheet. Then a sharps container with “≈ 25 injuries per 100 average daily census (2014)” and “up to $5,000 per incident” tags, and a strip of US lab statistics: about 14 billion tests a year in more than 266,000 CLIA-certified labs.

cues.text: Every hazardous chemical comes with a Safety Data Sheet. Under OSHA’s Hazard Communication rule it has 16 sections in a fixed order — and it must be in English.
Section 3 lists the ingredients. For a mixture, a hazardous ingredient usually counts at 1 percent or more. For carcinogens the cut-off is just 0.1 percent.
So 0.5 percent of a carcinogen counts, but 0.5 percent of a mild irritant may not. Low cut-offs protect against the worst hazards.
Sharps injuries are a constant risk. The reviewer cites about 25 injuries per 100 average daily census in 2014, and up to 5,000 dollars per incident for testing, treatment and counseling.
And the scale of it all: the CDC estimates about 14 billion lab tests a year in more than 266,000 CLIA-certified labs.

scenes.title: Law, guidance or target?
scenes.altText: Three sorting bins labelled “Federal rule”, “Guidance” and “Design target / reviewer figure”. Tokens drop in: “SDS in English” and “Eyewash within the work area” → Federal rule; “Reach eyewash in 10 s” → Guidance; “68–76 °F”, “12 air changes/h”, “2 exits >100 sq ft” → Design target. Then a licensure card: 12 states plus Puerto Rico (list dated 2017) require a state license in addition to national certification.

cues.text: Exams mix three kinds of numbers. Federal rules: the SDS in English, and eyewash facilities within the work area.
Guidance: reaching the eyewash within about 10 seconds. Design targets: temperature, humidity, air changes and the two-exit rule.

One more: licensure. A 2017 list shows 12 states plus Puerto Rico requiring a state license for lab staff. That is government permission to work — separate from national certification, which comes from a professional board.

props.title: Licensure: 12 states + Puerto Rico (list dated 2017)
lines: State license = permission to work there
Separate from national certification (e.g., ASCP BOC)

scenes.title: Ten seconds, one percent, point one
scenes.altText: Memory aid: three cards — “10 seconds” to the eyewash, “1%” as the usual SDS cut-off and “0.1%” for carcinogens — and a room token for 68–76 °F and about 12 air changes per hour. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: Ten to the eyewash. One percent to list. Point one if it can cause cancer.
And for the room: the comfort band, 68 to 76 degrees, about 12 air changes an hour.
Where it breaks: the cut-offs differ for some other hazard classes, the 10 seconds is guidance rather than OSHA law, and design numbers depend on local codes.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Law: SDS in English · eyewash in the work area”, “Guidance: reach it in 10 s”, “Targets: 68–76 °F, 12 air changes/h”.

cues.text: Sort lab numbers by source: OSHA law requires an English SDS and an eyewash within the work area, guidance says reach it in about 10 seconds, SDS cut-offs are usually 1% but 0.1% for carcinogens, and room temperature, air and exit figures are design targets set by local codes.

props.label: Law: SDS in English · eyewash within the work area
Guidance: reach the eyewash in ≈ 10 s

explanation.what: Plain language: a lab has to be comfortable and well aired, an eye-wash must be close enough to reach in seconds, every chemical comes with an information sheet in English, and some states require a license to work in a lab. Scientific terms: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.151(c) requires facilities for quick drenching or flushing within the work area for immediate emergency use; the Hazard Communication standard (29 CFR 1910.1200) requires a 16-section Safety Data Sheet in English, and its mixture classification uses cut-off values — generally 1%, 0.1% for carcinogens. Room temperature, humidity, air changes, space and exit counts are design targets.
explanation.why: Corrosive splashes injure eyes within seconds, so reach time matters more than distance. Very low cut-offs for carcinogens exist because tiny amounts can still pose a cancer risk. Steady temperature and humidity protect instruments, reagents and staff; frequent air changes dilute fumes. Licensure is a government permission to practice, so it is set state by state.
explanation.measure: Inspectors and safety officers check that eyewash units are in the work area and reachable quickly, that SDSs are present and in English, and that hazardous ingredients above cut-offs are listed. Facilities staff monitor temperature (68–76 °F), humidity (20–60%) and ventilation (≈ 12 air changes per hour) against the design.
explanation.differs: Law (OSHA text) vs guidance (OSHA letters, ANSI) vs design targets (reviewer figures, local codes). 1% vs 0.1% cut-off. Licensure (state, mandatory where it exists) vs certification (national professional board).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: how quickly an eyewash must be reachable (about 10 seconds), what replaced the MSDS (the SDS, in English, 16 sections), the 0.1% carcinogen cut-off, the comfort range 68–76 °F, about 12 air changes per hour, and how many states require licensure (12 plus Puerto Rico in the reviewer).

mnemonic.text: Ten to the eyewash; one percent to list; point one for cancer.
mnemonic.explanation: Reach the eyewash in about 10 seconds; hazardous mixture ingredients usually count at 1%; carcinogens count at 0.1%.
mnemonic.limitation: Some other hazard classes (e.g., Category 1 mutagens) also use 0.1%, and a few use other values. The 10 seconds is guidance, not OSHA regulation text, and room and exit numbers depend on local codes. The aid says nothing about licensure.

takeaway: Sort lab numbers by source: OSHA law requires an English SDS and an eyewash within the work area, guidance says reach it in about 10 seconds, SDS cut-offs are usually 1% but 0.1% for carcinogens, and room temperature, air and exit figures are design targets set by local codes.

questions.stem: A reagent mixture contains 0.5% of an ingredient classified as a carcinogen. Under OSHA Hazard Communication, how does this ingredient affect classification and the SDS?

options.text: It counts, because the carcinogen cut-off is 0.1%
options.rationale: Correct. Mixtures are classified as carcinogenic when a carcinogen ingredient is present at or above 0.1%, so 0.5% must be addressed.

options.text: It can be ignored, because it is below 1%
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 1% cut-off applies to many other hazards; carcinogens have a lower 0.1% cut-off.
Incorrect. No 5% cut-off applies to carcinogens; the value is 0.1%.

options.text: It matters only if the SDS is written in another language
options.rationale: Incorrect. Language is a separate rule — the SDS must be in English regardless.

questions.stem: Which statement about emergency eyewash placement is most accurate?

options.text: OSHA requires facilities within the work area for immediate use; guidance says they should be reachable in about 10 seconds
options.rationale: Correct. The regulation sets “within the work area”; OSHA interpretations and ANSI guidance add the 10-second reach.

options.text: OSHA regulation text requires exactly 100 feet
options.rationale: Incorrect. The regulation states no distance; 100 ft appears in a 1992 OSHA letter together with the 10-second reach.

options.text: Eyewash units belong in a separate room away from chemicals
options.rationale: Incorrect. A separate room would slow the response; they must be in the work area.

options.text: Reaching an eyewash within one minute is acceptable
options.rationale: Incorrect. Corrosive injury happens within seconds; guidance uses about 10 seconds.

questions.stem: A certified medical laboratory scientist moves to a state that requires laboratory personnel licensure. What applies?

options.text: They need the state license in addition to national certification
options.rationale: Correct. Licensure is a state government requirement to practice; certification is a separate credential from a professional board.

options.text: National certification automatically counts as the license
options.rationale: Incorrect. Certification may help qualify for a license, but it does not replace it.

options.text: Licensure is voluntary in states that have it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Where a state requires licensure, working without the license is not permitted.
Incorrect. Puerto Rico and a group of states (12 in a 2017 list) require it.
